p: York is the kind of city where you can fill three days and still not see everything, which is exactly why a bouncy break works so well in the middle. A good plan is to do one big indoor attraction in the morning, bounce after lunch when the little ones are starting to wilt, then finish with a gentle stroll and tea. Booking your Oxygen slot before you travel means you can build the rest of the day around it without any guesswork.

Train-mad kids will be in their element at the National Railway Museum, which is free to enter and sits just behind York station. It's full of famous locomotives, royal carriages and the kind of gleaming engines that stop grown-ups in their tracks too. JORVIK Viking Centre takes you back to the Viking-age city of Jorvik, complete with sights, sounds and, famously, smells. Clifford's Tower, perched on its grassy mound, gives you a great view over the rooftops for not much effort.

Got a sweet tooth in the family? York's Chocolate Story tells the tale of the city's big confectionery names and is a fun hour indoors. The Museum Gardens are free to wander, with the ruins of St Mary's Abbey dotted among the lawns and plenty of space for a picnic. Driving in? York's park-and-ride sites are a sensible way to dodge the city-centre traffic and parking headaches, leaving more energy for the trampolines and less for circling car parks. And if the weather does turn, the Minster's vast interior is a peaceful, awe-inspiring place to shelter for a while after all that noise.
